key_terms.meaning: ∇φ for a scalar field φ: a vector pointing the way φ rises fastest, of size equal to that maximum rate of rise
∇·F for a vector field F: outward flux per unit volume at a point, a scalar
∇×F: circulation of F per unit area at a point, a vector along the axis of rotation
∮F·dS over a closed surface = ∫(∇·F)dV over the volume inside it (Gauss's theorem)
∮F·dl around a closed loop = ∫(∇×F)·dS over any surface bounded by the loop
F = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r²) along the line joining two point charges, with ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m
E = F/q₀, the force per unit positive test charge at a point, in N/C or V/m
∮E·dS = Q_enclosed/ε₀ over any closed surface, in integral or ∇·E = ρ/ε₀ form
V = W/q, work per unit charge bringing a charge from infinity to the point; E = −∇V
∇²V = −ρ/ε₀, the potential equation where charge density ρ is present
∇²V = 0, the potential equation in a charge-free region
P = dipole moment per unit volume of a dielectric, in C/m²
D = ε₀E + P, so ∇·D = ρ_free and D = εE in a linear dielectric
ε_r = ε/ε₀, the factor by which a dielectric multiplies the permittivity; 1 for vacuum
dB = (μ₀I/4π)(dl × r̂)/r², with μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ T·m/A
∮B·dl = μ₀I_enclosed for steady currents, or μ₀I + μ₀ε₀ dΦ_E/dt with displacement current
emf = −dΦ_B/dt around a loop; the minus sign is Lenz's law
L = Φ_B/I for a coil, giving emf = −L dI/dt and stored energy ½LI²
I_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt, the current-equivalent term Maxwell added to Ampère's law
S = (1/μ₀) E × B, energy crossing unit area per second, in W/m²

takeaways: Vector calculus gives every field a local slope (gradient), a local source strength (divergence) and a local twist (curl), and the divergence and Stokes theorems turn these local numbers into integrals over volumes and surfaces.
Coulomb's law plus superposition is the whole of electrostatics; Gauss's law is the same physics rewritten in a form that makes symmetric problems one-line arithmetic.
Electric potential is a scalar that carries the same information as the field, and Poisson's and Laplace's equations give the field back from the charge distribution.
A dielectric does not supply free charge; its molecules become dipoles, the polarization P weakens the field inside, and D = ε₀E + P keeps track of free charge alone.
A steady current creates B with the right-hand rule; Ampère's law gives the field in one line whenever the current has enough symmetry.
Faraday's law says a changing magnetic flux drives charges round a loop, and the same law explains why a coil opposes changes in its own current.
Maxwell's four equations hold all classical electromagnetism once the displacement current is added to Ampère's law, and they predict that light is an electromagnetic wave.
In empty space E and B travel together in phase, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel, at speed c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s.
The Poynting vector gives the energy flow of a wave, and its average gives the intensity, which decides how much power an antenna or a cell phone receives.
bank_note: Syllabi stress derivations rather than statements: expect to derive Gauss's law results for standard symmetric shapes, get Poisson's equation from Gauss's law, and go all the way from Maxwell's equations to the wave equation and the Poynting theorem.

bank.q: Define the gradient of a scalar field and the divergence and curl of a vector field. State the divergence theorem and Stokes' theorem, and explain what each side of each theorem measures.
outline: gradient = vector with magnitude of maximum rate of change, direction of steepest ascent
divergence = outward flux per unit volume, a scalar
curl = circulation per unit area, a vector
divergence theorem: surface integral of F over a closed surface equals volume integral of ∇·F
Stokes' theorem: line integral of F around a closed loop equals surface integral of ∇×F
meaning: sources and circulation of a field are fixed by local derivatives

bank.q: State Coulomb's law in vector form for two point charges in free space. Define the electric field and state the superposition principle.
outline: F = q₁q₂ r̂/(4πε₀r²), with ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m
like charges repel, unlike attract, force along the line of centres
E = F/q₀ in N/C
superposition: total E is the vector sum of the fields of individual charges
note the inverse-square dependence and the role of the medium (ε = ε₀ε_r)

bank.q: State Gauss's law in integral and differential form. Explain why it is useful for computing fields only for charge distributions with symmetry.
outline: ∮E·dS = Q_enc/ε₀ and ∇·E = ρ/ε₀
flux depends only on enclosed charge, not on the shape of the surface
to pull E out of the integral, E must be constant in magnitude and normal to a chosen surface
hence the sphere, cylinder and plane are the standard cases
no symmetry means the integral must be done the hard way

bank.q: Define electric potential and explain why it is a scalar while the electric field is a vector. Write Poisson's and Laplace's equations and state what each term means.
outline: V = W/q, work per unit charge from infinity
V is a scalar; E = −∇V recovers the vector field
a scalar plus one differentiation carries all three components of E
Poisson: ∇²V = −ρ/ε₀ with ρ the volume charge density in C/m³
Laplace: ∇²V = 0 where ρ = 0
helps solve problems with conductors held at fixed potentials

bank.q: Define polarization P, electric displacement D and susceptibility χ_e. Explain how bound charges appear on the faces of a polarized dielectric slab.
outline: P = dipole moment per unit volume, C/m²
P = ε₀χ_e E and ε_r = 1 + χ_e
D = ε₀E + P, with ∇·D = ρ_free
inside the slab the dipoles cancel; at the surfaces one sign is left over
surface bound charge density σ_b = P·n̂
the bound charge creates a field opposing the applied field, reducing E inside by ε_r

bank.q: State Faraday's law of induction and Lenz's law. Define self-inductance and mutual inductance and write the energy stored in an inductor.
outline: emf = −dΦ_B/dt, with Φ_B = ∫B·dS in Wb
Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change in flux
motional emf = Bvl for a rod moving perpendicular to B
L = Φ_B/I in henry; emf = −L dI/dt
mutual inductance M: flux in one coil per unit current in the other
energy stored U = ½LI²

bank.q: A sphere of radius R carries a uniform volume charge density ρ. Using Gauss's law, find the electric field and potential at a point inside the sphere and at a point outside it.
outline: spherical symmetry: take a Gaussian sphere of radius r
outside (r > R): E = Q/(4πε₀r²) with Q = (4/3)πR³ρ
inside (r < R): E = ρr/(3ε₀), linear in r
potential outside: V = Q/(4πε₀r)
potential inside: integrate E inward from R and get V = (ρ/6ε₀)(3R² − r²)
check continuity of V at r = R

bank.q: Derive the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor when a dielectric slab of thickness t and relative permittivity ε_r fills part of the gap. Find the energy stored for a given charge and comment on the result.
outline: treat the filled and unfilled parts as two capacitors in series
E in the dielectric is E₀/ε_r for the same free charge
V = E₀(d − t) + (E₀/ε_r)t
C = ε₀A/[d − t + t/ε_r]
energy U = Q²/2C, so the dielectric increases stored energy at fixed Q
limiting checks: t = 0 and t = d

bank.q: A coaxial cable carries a steady current I up the inner conductor and back down the outer conductor. Use Ampère's law to find B in the three regions and sketch its variation with distance.
outline: cylindrical symmetry: circular Amperian loops about the axis
inside the inner conductor (r < a): B = μ₀Ir/(2πa²)
between the conductors (a < r < b): B = μ₀I/(2πr)
outside the cable (r > c): enclosed current is zero, so B = 0
show B continuous at the conductor surfaces
note the 1/r fall in the gap and the right-hand-rule direction

bank.q: A metal rod of length L slides with constant speed v on two parallel rails in a uniform magnetic field B perpendicular to the plane of the rails. Find the induced emf, the current, the force needed to keep the rod moving, and the power dissipated.
outline: flux Φ_B = BLx, so emf = BLv
current I = BLv/R for a circuit resistance R
Lenz's law fixes the direction: the field of the induced current opposes the motion
magnetic force on the rod = BIL = B²L²v/R, opposite to v
mechanical power = Fv = B²L²v²/R, equal to I²R
energy conservation check

bank.q: Starting from Maxwell's equations in free space, derive the wave equation for E and for B, and show that the wave speed is c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀).
outline: take the curl of ∇×E = −∂B/∂t
use ∇×B = μ₀ε₀ ∂E/∂t and ∇·E = 0
use the identity ∇×(∇×E) = ∇(∇·E) − ∇²E
get ∇²E = μ₀ε₀ ∂²E/∂t², and the same for B
compare with ∇²E = (1/c²)∂²E/∂t²
insert μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ and ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² to get c ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s

bank.q: Show that Ampère's law in the form ∮B·dl = μ₀I fails for a capacitor being charged. Introduce the displacement current, write the Ampère–Maxwell law, and show it is consistent with charge conservation.
outline: pick a loop round the wire and two surfaces bounded by it
flat surface gives μ₀I; balloon surface through the capacitor gives zero enclosed current
contradiction: the field between the plates is real and measurable
Maxwell's fix: add I_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt
check that ε₀ dΦ_E/dt equals the conduction current I for the capacitor
take divergence of ∇×B = μ₀J + μ₀ε₀ ∂E/∂t to recover ∇·J = −∂ρ/∂t

bank.q: Derive the Poynting theorem from Maxwell's equations, state the meaning of each term, and use the Poynting vector to find the intensity of a plane electromagnetic wave of amplitude E₀.
outline: start from E·(∇×H) − H·(∇×E)
substitute Maxwell's curl equations
obtain ∂u/∂t + ∇·S = −J·E, with u = ½ε₀E² + ½B²/μ₀
S = (1/μ₀)E×B is energy flow per unit area per second
plane wave: B = E/c and E, B perpendicular
average S = ½ε₀cE₀², equal to E₀B₀/(2μ₀)

bank.q: Derive the boundary conditions obeyed by the normal and tangential components of E, D, B and H at an interface between two media. Use them to explain why a good conductor reflects electromagnetic waves strongly.
outline: pillbox across the surface: normal B is continuous, normal D jumps by σ_free
loop across the surface: tangential E is continuous, tangential H jumps by surface current
apply with E = 0 inside a good conductor
conduction current kills the transmitted wave within a skin depth
the reflected wave carries most of the energy
link this to a metal coating being an electromagnetic shield

glossary.def: A quantity with one value at each point in space, such as temperature or electric potential.
A quantity with a magnitude and a direction at each point in space, such as electric field or current density.
The integral ∫F·dS of a field over a surface, counting how much of the field passes through it.
The line integral ∮F·dl of a field around a closed loop, measuring how much the field pushes round the loop.
The three-dimensional version of an angle, measured in steradians; the whole sphere is 4π sr.
A field whose circulation round every closed loop is zero, so it can be written as the gradient of a potential.
A surface on which the potential has the same value everywhere; the field is normal to it.
A pair of equal and opposite charges a small distance apart, with moment p = qd pointing from −q to +q.
Charge that appears on a dielectric because its dipoles line up, not because charge was added.
Charge placed on a conductor or dielectric from outside, the charge a battery supplies.
The constant χ_e in P = ε₀χ_eE; it measures how strongly a dielectric polarizes.
C = Q/V in farad, the charge a conductor pair holds per volt of potential difference.
The potential difference at which a dielectric suddenly conducts and sparks.
The vector B, in tesla, that gives the force qv×B on a moving charge.
The rule that the field of a current circles the wire in the sense your right-hand fingers curl when the thumb points along the current.
The vector A with B = ∇×A, useful because ∇·B = 0 always holds.
A long coil of wire in which the magnetic field is nearly uniform inside and about zero outside.
Φ_B = ∫B·dS over a surface, measured in weber.
The induced current flows in the direction that opposes the change of flux that produced it.
Circulating induced current in a bulk conductor placed in a changing magnetic field.
The distance over which a wave's amplitude falls to 1/e of its surface value inside a conductor.
The term ε₀ dΦ_E/dt that acts like a current wherever the electric flux changes.
Four equations relating E, B, their sources and their time derivatives; they govern all classical electromagnetic behaviour.
The earlier time t − r/c at which a source must act for its effect to reach a point a distance r away now.
